assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED opened a genuinely new regime: single microwave photons strongly coupled to a controllable superconducting artificial atom in a one-dimensional, engineerable environment. It supplied the dispersive readout, the bus and the coupling architecture on which nearly all superconducting-qubit work and much of microwave quantum optics (including waveguide QED and giant atoms) rests. The discovery is the platform physics, not the later computer, and that is a clean, original, lasting contribution. It also extends the 2025 prize logically, which was for macroscopic quantum effects in circuits, without duplicating it.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and its first experimental realisation (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are decisive. The supplied credit supports a fair configuration of Schoelkopf as experimental leader plus the theorists Blais and Girvin. Allocation between Blais and Girvin and the experimental side, notably Andreas Wallraff who is not in the credited names, is a real issue. As far as I recall, Wallraff was central to the first strong-coupling experiment, so a three-person set drawn only from the supplied names may omit a decisive contributor.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: reproduced and extended in dozens of laboratories over twenty years, the interpretation is stable, and it underpins a whole industry. Timing is good, and since the 2025 prize for circuit quantum effects there is a natural continuity rather than a premature call.
uncertainties: Wallraff is not among the credited names, so the allocation within the supplied strings is imperfect.
Possible perception of overlap with the 2025 circuit-quantum prize.

I have a field and institutional proximity (superconducting circuits, WACQT), so my enthusiasm should be discounted and the committee should check my judgement against colleagues; I have not independently verified the exact credit history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller provided the theoretical foundation for quantum computing with trapped ions (the 1995 gate proposal) and for quantum simulation with ultracold atoms and ions, including the Hubbard-model proposal for optical lattices and Rydberg gates. These proposals defined the experimental programmes of many laboratories and gave quantum information a physical, controllable implementation. The originality and the breadth of influence are very high, and the ideas carry across ions, atoms and, indirectly, circuits.
assessment.attribution: A two-person award is natural and the two names are the clear and well-known core of this contribution. Credit with experimentalists (Wineland, Blatt, Monroe, Bloch and others) is partly addressed by earlier prizes and could be argued either way. The pairing is clean.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Trapped-ion gates and analogue and digital quantum simulation have been realised and confirmed by multiple groups over three decades. Timing is arguably overdue.
uncertainties: The overlap with the optical-lattice quantum simulation candidate and with the 2012 prize for individual quantum systems could make the committee treat this as already partly recognised.
A theory-only award for a field whose experiments were rewarded earlier needs a clear statement of the specific discovery being cited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, with Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and Ye's strontium clocks, achieved 10^-18 fractional systematic uncertainty. This is a clean case of a quantum-controlled experiment where every physical detail (blackbody shifts, lattice light shifts, collisions) is understood and controlled. It enables tests of fundamental constants and relativity at the centimetre-to-millimetre level and relativistic geodesy, and it motivates redefining the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori (magic-wavelength concept and early realisation) and Ye (precision demonstration, spectroscopy and many-body clock physics) are a clear and compact pair. Other contributors (for example Hall and Hänsch for the comb, who were already rewarded in 2005) are not needed. A fair two-person configuration is available from the supplied names.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by several national laboratories and groups; reproducibility is excellent. Timely, especially if the SI second redefinition proceeds, although the clock community might still regard further improvement as ongoing.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as discovery physics or as precision engineering building on the earlier comb prize.
Further ion-clock competitors and the exact priority split are matters I am not certain of.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction at the magic angle, followed by the 2018 experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene, opened moire quantum matter as a tunable platform for correlated and topological phases. The idea is original, the experimental demonstration was striking, and the field has grown enormously. This lies outside my core expertise, so I defer partially to condensed-matter colleagues.
assessment.attribution: Theory prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald) plus the experimental discovery (Jarillo-Herrero, with Cao and others in his group) fit a three-person prize. Notably early contributions by other groups (for example Yuan Cao as a student, Dean, Young, Yazdani, Efetov and others) raise questions, but the supplied set is a defensible core.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature: the central phenomena have been reproduced in many groups, but the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, and sample-dependence is a concern. Recognition could be considered slightly early, but impact is already large.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted graphene remains unsettled.
Sample variability and reproducibility of details across groups.
The credit boundary with other early experimental contributors is unclear to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerance theory established, against widespread scepticism, that arbitrarily long quantum computation is possible in principle with noisy hardware, and the surface and toric code framework is the central target of today's superconducting-qubit roadmaps. Conceptually this is one of the most significant ideas in quantum information. From a practical standpoint, my own programme depends on it, and I stress that threshold-level, below-break-even error correction has only recently begun to be demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Shor (first code and fault-tolerant ideas), Steane (independent code construction), and Kitaev (topological codes and anyons) are plausible core figures. Others such as Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Preskill, Aharonov and Ben-Or, Bravyi are also widely cited, so the allocation is genuinely contested, and a three-person limit leaves a notable list of omissions.
assessment.maturity: Theoretically settled, but experimental confirmation is still early (small logical-qubit demonstrations beyond break-even only in the last few years). A prize for this may be premature as a physical discovery, and I would be cautious about rewarding promise rather than demonstrated physics.
uncertainties: Credit is distributed among many theorists, so a three-person selection is fragile.
Whether the prize would be for physics discovery or for a mathematical and computer-science idea.
The experimental demonstration is not yet mature enough for a firm view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light, proposed by Caves for interferometric gravitational-wave detection and demonstrated in the lab by Kimble and others, enables measurement below the standard quantum limit. It is now used in the operating LIGO and Virgo detectors, which makes the quantum-optics result visible in an actual large-scale instrument. It is original and has a clear lasting impact, and it is a cleanly defined quantum phenomenon made controllable.
assessment.attribution: Caves (1981 proposal) and Kimble (first squeezed-state generation and later applications) are central; Slusher, Wu and Walls also did early experimental squeezing and are not in the supplied set. The roles of Schnabel and Mavalvala in implementing squeezing in detectors are strong but of a different type, so I would choose Caves, Kimble and Schnabel, and recognise that the supplied credit does not capture the early squeezing experimenters.
assessment.maturity: Mature: squeezed-light enhancement is now routine in the gravitational-wave detectors, independently confirmed in GEO600 and LIGO. Timely. The central physics predates the application by decades.
uncertainties: Early experimental squeezing credit (Slusher and colleagues) is missing from the supplied names, so attribution is incomplete.
Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from the 2017 gravitational-wave prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable arrays of individually trapped neutral atoms with Rydberg-mediated interactions are a leading platform for analogue and digital quantum simulation and computing, and they have exposed new many-body phases and small-scale error-corrected logical operations. The experimental control and the high-fidelity gates are impressive and based on a well-understood quantum optics toolbox.
assessment.attribution: Lukin, Browaeys and Saffman cover the early blockade-gate proposals and the main array experiments, but the field is very recent and large, with major contributions from Bernien and Greiner, Lukin's collaborators, Browaeys and Lahaye, Bloch, Weiss, Regal, Endres and others. Allocation is not yet settled.
assessment.maturity: Rapidly maturing but still developing; the key demonstrations are within the last decade, and the computing claims are still being independently benchmarked. Recognition now would be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse in a young field.
Scalability and fidelity claims are still being benchmarked by other groups.
Overlap with other AMO quantum-simulation candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Light-matter quantum interfaces underpin quantum memories, atom-photon entanglement and the first elements of quantum networks, including cavity QED single-atom control (Rempe, Kimble) and atomic-ensemble memories (Lukin). The physics is important and nicely connected to my interest in photon-matter coupling in the microwave domain, but the candidate is a compound topic of several distinct achievements.
assessment.attribution: Kimble, Rempe and Lukin each led substantive, independent lines (cavity QED, quantum state transfer, ensemble memories). The credit is plausible, but no single discovery is cleanly specified. A prize would need a sharper definition of what is being cited, and several others (Polzik, Kuzmich, Cirac, Duan, Zoller) are plausible.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation of the individual components; however, the quantum network remains a multi-year engineering target, so the unifying claim is only partially mature.
uncertainties: The candidate is a compound discovery and may need a narrower formulation.
Overlap of Kimble and Lukin with other candidates on my ballot.
Real-world quantum networks are not yet demonstrated at scale.
